meta.location: The land of Zarahemla; the river Sidon

world_behind.title: The chapter is an interruption, and it announces itself as one
world_behind.text: Verse 13 opens "Now we will return again to the Amlicites," which means the writer knows he has left them. Between verse 4 and verse 13 he stops the war story to explain where a mark came from, then picks the Amlicites back up. The digression is why the chapter exists.

world_behind.title: The war's civilian bill, itemized first
world_behind.text: Verse 2 lists what the fighting cost before the chapter says anything about marks: women and children killed with the sword, flocks and herds, and fields of grain trodden down by the hosts of men. The damage to the crop is incidental (nobody aimed at it), and the record counts it anyway.

world_behind.title: A stock description, reused decades later
world_behind.text: The picture in verse 5 is not composed for this chapter. Twenty years on, at the battle with Zerahemnah, the record reaches for the same clauses in nearly the same order to describe a different army. What looks like observation is a formula the abridgment keeps on hand.

world_behind.title: Red, and where they put it
world_behind.text: The Amlicites chose a color and chose the most legible place on a body. Forehead marks run through scripture in both directions. Ezekiel's men who sigh and cry (Ezek. 9:4) are marked there so they will be spared, and Revelation's (Rev. 13:16) are marked there to show whose they are. A mark on the forehead is not for the wearer to see.

world_behind.title: This passage has a reception history worth naming
world_behind.text: Verses 6 through 9 have been read as a statement about skin color and race. The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints "disavows the theories advanced in the past that black skin is a sign of divine disfavor or curse, or that it reflects unrighteous actions in a premortal life," and teaches that "all are alike unto God." The chapter's own definitions in verses 10, 11 and 19 point the same direction: category by belief, consequence by choice.

world_behind.title: The record pauses to say who kept it
world_behind.text: Verse 12 is a sentence about sources: it is they who have kept the records which are true, of their own people and also of the Lamanites. In the middle of describing two nations, the writer notes that only one of them was writing this down, and that it undertook to write about both.

world_behind.title: One year, from start to finish
world_behind.text: Verse 25 says all of it was commenced and ended inside a single twelvemonth of the new calendar: the election, the secession, two battles, a foreign invasion. The dead are given as thousands and tens of thousands, one chapter after the record counted them to the single soul.

words.text: Trampled flat. The verse applies it to fields of grain destroyed "by the hosts of men," which makes the damage incidental. Nobody set out to ruin the crop. The record uses the phrase seven times, mostly of vineyards and of people; this is the only place it names food.

Cut close, sheared. The word arrives twice in two verses, first as something the Amlicites did not do and then as something the Lamanites did. The chapter is measuring one group against another by grooming, and the negative comes first: they marked themselves, nevertheless they had not shorn their heads.

Bound around, belted on. The Lamanite description turns on it twice: a skin girded about the loins, armor girded about them. The record uses the verb seven times, from Laban's sword to Moroni's breastplate. It is the vocabulary of what a man straps on before a fight.

Of or belonging to the house of Ishmael. The word is unique in scripture, and it exists because the sentence is being careful about who is included. The list runs Laman and Lemuel, the sons of Ishmael, and the Ishmaelitish women. Precision about lineage is being used to name a group.

To mix, to combine so that the parts are no longer separate. "Mingle his seed" appears once in scripture. The verb is doing genealogical work in verse 9 and the chapter immediately reframes it in verse 10 as a matter of being led away, something a person does.

Accurate, matching the facts. It is applied here to a tradition rather than to a doctrine: those who believed the records brought out of Jerusalem "and also in the tradition of their fathers, which were correct." The chapter's dividing line is a question about whether an inherited account is true.

To harvest. The verse uses it twice in one sentence: souls sent to the eternal world "that they might reap their rewards according to their works," and then "to reap eternal happiness or eternal misery." The figure makes the outcome a crop that was planted earlier, which is the same argument verse 19 made about curses.

phrases.term: The number of the slain were not numbered, because of the greatness of their number
phrases.text: A sentence that says the same word three times and gives up. One chapter earlier the record produced exact totals for both armies. Here the arithmetic collapses inside a single clause, and the construction turns up twice more in the book and once in Mormon's own war, always at the point where a war stops being countable.

phrases.term: Their bones are in the depths of the sea
phrases.text: The bodies Alma threw off the bank in the previous chapter, followed to where they ended up. "The depths of the sea" is the phrase the record used for Lehi's family nearly drowning on the voyage over. Here it is a grave, and the last three words ("and they are many") are the whole elegy.

phrases.term: After the manner of the Lamanites
phrases.text: Partial imitation, and the verse is careful about the limits. They copied the manner and not the whole of it. The red went on, the hair stayed. Whatever the Amlicites were doing, it was a quotation rather than a conversion, and the sentence ends on what they declined to copy.

phrases.term: That their seed might be distinguished from the seed of their brethren
phrases.text: The stated purpose, and it is preservative rather than punitive: so that the two would not mix and take up traditions that would destroy them. The verse gives a reason where it could have given a verdict, and the reason is about what people would come to believe.

Filed under that heading. The whole verse is about a person who "suffered himself to be led away," and the passive is doing real work: he allowed it. Whatever else the chapter says about marks, it defines membership by a decision, twice, in consecutive verses.

phrases.term: Yea, they set the mark upon themselves
phrases.text: The chapter's hinge, and the "yea" is Mormon insisting. He has just said the Amlicites had a mark set upon them; then he corrects the impression before it can settle. They did it. Four words later he names the color and the place on the body.

The writer stepping out from behind the narrative to say what he wants understood, and then widening it past the Amlicites entirely. The sentence ends by making the rule true of everyone in that condition. A rule about curses, offered by the man who has just spent six verses quoting one.

phrases.term: Every man receiveth wages of him whom he listeth to obey
phrases.text: Employment as the figure for allegiance. You are not punished by the master you chose; you are paid by him. The construction appears once elsewhere in scripture, in John, where the reaper receives wages and gathers fruit unto life eternal. It is the same exchange, running the other way.

verses.label: v. 1–3
verses.title: After the battle
verses.text: The survivors bury the dead and go home to their lands, their houses, their wives and children. Women and children had been killed too, and flocks, and fields trampled by armies. The bodies thrown into Sidon are followed to the sea. Three verses of accounting, and the first of them refuses to produce a number.

verses.label: v. 4–5
verses.title: Two descriptions, set side by side
verses.text: The Amlicites marked themselves with red on their foreheads after the manner of the Lamanites, but did not shave their heads. Then the Lamanites: heads shorn, a skin about the loins, armor, bows, arrows, stones, slings. The comparison is exact about what was copied and what was not.

verses.label: v. 6–9
verses.title: The older account, and the reason given for it
verses.text: The account reaches back four hundred years, names the four families it applies to, and ties the curse to their having sought to destroy their brethren, whom the verse pauses to call just and holy men. Verse 8 supplies the purpose: so the two seeds would not mix and take on traditions that would destroy them. Verse 9 extends the same consequence to anyone who crossed over.

verses.label: v. 10–12
verses.title: Who counts as which
verses.text: The record replaces descent with a two-part test and states both halves in the same construction. One side is defined by a single act, "whosoever suffered himself to be led away by the Lamanites was called under that head." The other takes four conditions: not believing the Lamanite tradition, believing "those records which were brought out of the land of Jerusalem," believing the correct tradition of the fathers, and keeping the commandments. Verse 12 then names the function that follows, "it is they who have kept the records which are true of their people, and also of the people of the Lamanites." Jacob 1:14 drew the same line by a different criterion, friendliness to Nephi, four hundred years earlier in the record.

verses.label: v. 13–19
verses.title: Mormon steps forward
verses.text: Mormon returns to them and immediately makes the correction that matters: the mark was self-applied. Then the promises to Nephi in four clauses. Then the two sentences he wrote the chapter to write: they did not know they were fulfilling anything, and they brought the curse on themselves, as everyone does.

verses.label: v. 20–24
verses.title: A second army, and a chief judge who stays home
verses.text: Not many days later another Lamanite army comes to the same place. Alma is wounded and does not go up. He sends an army instead; they drive the Lamanites out and come back, and there is peace for a time. The verse about his wound is one line long and the record does not return to it.

verses.label: v. 25–27
verses.title: One year, and the wages
verses.text: The record dates the whole sequence to a single year, "commenced and ended in the fifth year of the reign of the judges," and then gives the casualties as an order of magnitude rather than a figure, "thousands and tens of thousands of souls." Verse 27 supplies a general principle in the middle of a battle summary, "every man receiveth wages of him whom he listeth to obey," and attributes it, "according to the words of the spirit of prophecy." The chapter then closes on the same date it opened the paragraph with, so a statement about eternal wages is bracketed on both sides by the fifth year of the judges.

chapter.title: The chapter distinguishes the mark from the curse, and gives the rule for reading it
chapter.text: The curse is separation and the mark makes separation visible; verse 19 supplies the interpretation in the author's own voice. The cursed bring it on themselves, and so does every man who is cursed. The passage that has been read hardest as a statement about bodies contains, in its own middle, a statement about choices.

chapter.title: Membership is defined confessionally, twice, in consecutive verses
chapter.text: Verse 10 files a man by what he allowed; verse 11 files him by what he believed and kept. Neither definition mentions ancestry, and both are stated in the passage where ancestry is under discussion. Forty chapters later the record will say plainly that the Zoramites became Lamanites.

chapter.title: The Amlicites do to themselves what the chapter says was done to the Lamanites
chapter.text: Verse 13 states who applied it: "they set the mark upon themselves, yea, even a mark of red upon their foreheads." Verse 14 quotes the older sentence being fulfilled, "I will set a mark on them that they and their seed may be separated." Verse 18 records that the men doing it did not know, "the Amlicites knew not that they were fulfilling the words of God." Verse 19 draws the general rule in the record's own voice, "they brought upon themselves the curse; and even so doth every man that is cursed bring upon himself his own condemnation." A category the chapter elsewhere treats as inherited is entered here by an act of paint.

chapter.title: Mormon quotes a revelation that survives nowhere else in full
chapter.text: Verses 14 through 17 give four promises to Nephi in the Lord's voice, joined by "and again." Pieces appear in 2 Nephi 5; the sequence as a block does not. The chapter is preserving a document.

chapter.title: The counting stops, and the chapter says why
chapter.text: Alma 2 gave twelve thousand five hundred thirty-two and six thousand five hundred sixty-two. Verse 1 here cannot produce a figure; verse 26 offers "thousands and tens of thousands." A war that was still an accountable event two chapters ago is now reported only in orders of magnitude.

chapter.title: A one-line wound with consequences
chapter.text: Verse 22 reports that Alma was afflicted with a wound and did not go up to battle, and the record never mentions it again. It is the first time the chief judge delegates a campaign, and the next chapter has him giving up the judgment-seat entirely.

chapter.title: The chapter ends inside Benjamin's vocabulary
chapter.text: "Open rebellion against God," "listeth to obey," and wages paid by a chosen master all come out of one sermon at the temple in Zarahemla, forty years earlier. Mormon reaches for a king's sermon to close an account of people who wanted a king.

chapter.title: Role in the book
chapter.text: Alma 3 completes the fifth year and sets three things running: the Amlicite-Lamanite alliance that keeps returning, the definition of Nephite that the Zoramite chapters will need, and a chief judge worn down enough that Alma 4 can hand the office away.

applications.title: Notice who applied the mark
applications.text: The chapter's whole correction is that these men marked themselves. Before treating a difference as something that happened to someone, it is worth asking whether it was chosen, and the answer changes what you owe them either way.

applications.title: Read the author's own gloss before your own
applications.text: Mormon does not leave the passage open; he says what he wants understood and then extends it to everyone. When a text supplies its own rule for reading, that rule outranks the reading you arrived with.

applications.title: Define your people by what they believe
applications.text: The record had every opportunity to draw the line by ancestry and drew it by conviction and by the records kept. Groups that define themselves confessionally can be joined and left; groups that define themselves by birth cannot.

applications.title: Watch the word "suffered" (v. 10).
applications.text: Whoever suffered himself to be led away. He was not dragged; he allowed it. Most drift is permitted, and permission is still a decision.

applications.title: Ask what you are being paid, and by whom
applications.text: Wages come from the master you listed to obey. The metaphor is unsentimental: nobody is being punished by a stranger, everyone is being paid by an employer they picked.

applications.title: Count while counting is still possible
applications.text: Two chapters ago the record gave exact figures. Here the number defeats the writer. Losses usually stay countable for a while before they stop, and the honest accounting is the early one.

applications.title: Let the wound be reported and let it change the plan
applications.text: Alma was hurt, so he sent someone else and stayed home. One line, no apology, no explanation. The campaign still succeeded.

questions.text: What have I marked myself with lately, and who was it meant to be legible to?
What have I suffered myself to be led away by, without ever deciding to go?
If my people were defined by what I actually believe and keep, would I still be in it?
Where have I described as done-to-me something I did to myself?
What condemnation am I carrying that I brought along with me?
Who is paying me, and would I say so out loud?
